hypothesis: The neuron responds selectively to **prominent, elongated linear structures or high-contrast boundaries** oriented horizontally or gently diagonally. These features consistently manifest as solid dark bands (such as wings, insect bodies, wires) or sharp interfaces where bright highlights meet deep shadows (such as metallic rims, wave crests, or architectural edges). The activating elements are defined by stark luminance contrast, typically composed of **jet black, dark charcoal, or deep shadow** paired with **bright white, silver, or pale gray**. The background is uniformly desaturated, usually consisting of **flat fields of light-to-medium gray** or textured concrete. The neuron remains invariant to object identity and material properties, responding equally to biological silhouettes and metallic reflections as long as the continuous, extended edge is preserved. The activating feature typically occupies **10–30% of the vertical image space while spanning 50–100% of the horizontal width**, often dividing the composition across the center or upper thirds.
